title: Python, Programs and Output
summary: Understand how Python programs execute and write your first useful scripts.
definition: Python is a programming language: you write instructions, Python executes them in order, and each instruction changes program state. Learn the edit-run-debug cycle and how expressions become values.
codeExample: print("Hello, Python!")
howItWorks: Python executes statements in order unless control flow changes that order.
print() sends a value to the program output.
Expressions produce values; statements perform actions.
Good programmers run small changes often and read errors instead of guessing.
fullExample:
print("PyPath Python Challenge")
name = "Alex"
print("Welcome,", name)
print("Today I am learning Python.")
practiceTask: Write a short introduction program that prints your name, a goal, and one sentence explaining why you want to learn Python.
starterCode:
print("My name is ...")
print("My goal is ...")
print("I am learning Python because ...")

title: Variables and State
summary: Store information, update it, and choose readable names.
definition: A variable is a name bound to a value. Assignment creates or changes a binding; it does not mean mathematical equality. Names make program state readable and reusable.
codeExample:
score = 10
score += 5
print(score)
howItWorks: Use descriptive snake_case names.
Assignment stores a value in a name.
Variables can be reassigned to values of different types, although consistent types are usually clearer.
Augmented assignment such as += updates existing state.
fullExample:
name = "Alex"
age = 20
balance = 100.0
balance += 25
print(name, age, balance)
practiceTask: Create variables for a product name, price, quantity, and discount. Calculate and print the final total.
starterCode:
product = "Notebook"
price = 5.0
quantity = 3
discount = 0.10
# Calculate the final total here

title: Types, Conversion and Truth
summary: Work confidently with strings, numbers, booleans, None, and type conversion.
definition: Python values have types. Common built-ins include str, int, float, bool, and None. Convert values explicitly when data arrives from input or another system.
codeExample:
age_text = "21"
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 1)
howItWorks: input() returns text, even when the user types a number.
int(), float(), and str() perform explicit conversion.
bool values are True or False; None represents absence of a value.
Use type() while learning or debugging, but prefer clear program design over excessive type checks.
fullExample:
raw = "42"
number = int(raw)
price = 12.5
available = True
nothing = None
print(number, type(number).__name__)
print(price, available, nothing)
practiceTask: Read a number stored as text, convert it safely, calculate its square, and print whether the result is even.
starterCode:
text = "24"
number = int(text)
# Calculate and print the square
# Print whether it is even

title: Strings and Text Processing
summary: Build and transform text using indexing, slicing, methods, and f-strings.
definition: Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Python provides indexing, slicing, methods, and formatted string literals for clear text processing.
codeExample:
name = "python"
print(name.upper())
print(f"Learning {name}")
howItWorks: Indexing reads one character; slicing reads a range.
Methods such as strip(), lower(), upper(), replace(), and split() create useful transformed values.
f-strings embed expressions directly into readable output.
Because strings are immutable, string operations return new strings.
fullExample:
text = "  Python Developer  "
clean = text.strip()
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.replace("Developer", "Engineer"))
name = "Sam"
print(f"{name} is learning Python.")
practiceTask: Clean a messy sentence, count a chosen character, create a list of words with split(), and print a formatted summary.
starterCode:

title: Operators and Expressions
summary: Use arithmetic, comparison, logical, membership, identity, and precedence rules.
definition: Operators combine values into expressions. Arithmetic operators calculate, comparison operators produce booleans, and logical operators combine conditions. Understand precedence and use parentheses when clarity matters.
codeExample:
total = 10 + 5 * 2
is_valid = total > 15 and total < 30
print(total, is_valid)
howItWorks: * and / bind more tightly than + and -; use parentheses when an expression could be misunderstood.
== compares values; is is primarily for object identity.
in tests membership.
and, or, and not combine boolean conditions with short-circuit evaluation.
fullExample:
price = 80
quantity = 3
subtotal = price * quantity
discounted = subtotal >= 200 and quantity >= 3
print(subtotal)
print("Discount:", discounted)
practiceTask: Build a bill calculation that uses arithmetic, comparisons, and boolean logic to decide whether a customer qualifies for a discount.
starterCode:

quantity = 3
# Calculate the bill and discount rule

title: Conditions and Branching
summary: Make programs choose different actions with if, elif, and else.
definition: Conditional statements select code based on boolean expressions. Good branching handles normal cases, boundaries, and invalid input explicitly.
howItWorks: if tests the first condition.
elif checks additional conditions only when earlier conditions failed.
else handles the remaining case.
Indentation defines the block, so consistent indentation is part of Python syntax.
practiceTask: Create a grade classifier with A/B/C/D/F ranges. Test normal values and boundary values such as 59, 60, 79, and 80.

title: Loops and Repetition
summary: Repeat work with for and while loops and understand loop state.
definition: Loops automate repeated work. for iterates over an iterable; while repeats while a condition remains true. Correct loop conditions and state updates prevent accidental infinite loops.
codeExample:
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)
howItWorks: for is ideal when iterating over a known sequence or range.
while is useful when repetition depends on a changing condition.
range() produces a sequence of integers lazily.
Track loop state clearly and ensure while conditions can eventually become false.
fullExample:
total = 0
for number in range(1, 11):
    total += number
print("Total:", total)

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
practiceTask: Write a program that calculates the sum of numbers 1–100, then write a while loop that counts down from 10.

title: Loop Control and Validation
summary: Use break, continue, nested loops, and validation patterns without creating fragile loops.
definition: break exits the nearest loop; continue skips to the next iteration. Validation loops repeatedly request acceptable input until a condition is satisfied.
howItWorks: break is useful when the required result has been found.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration.
Nested loops solve repeated work across multiple dimensions but can become expensive.
Validation loops should make progress toward a valid state and provide a clear exit.
fullExample:
secret = 7
attempts = 0
while True:
    attempts += 1
    guess = 7
    if guess == secret:
        print("Correct after", attempts, "attempt(s)")
        break
practiceTask: Build a small input-validation loop: keep asking for a positive integer until the user enters one, then report it.

title: Functions, Scope and Return Values
summary: Design reusable functions with parameters, return values, local scope, and clear responsibilities.
definition: A function packages behavior behind a name. Parameters receive input, return sends a result to the caller, and local variables normally belong to the function call.
howItWorks: Define a function once and call it many times.
Prefer return values for reusable logic; print at the program boundary.
Local variables prevent unrelated code from depending on hidden state.
Keep functions focused: one clear job is easier to test and reuse.
practiceTask: Create functions for validation, calculation, and formatting in a mini bill program. Make each function return data instead of printing internally.

title: Lists, Tuples and Sequence Operations
summary: Store ordered collections and use indexing, slicing, mutation, unpacking, and iteration.
definition: Lists are mutable ordered collections; tuples are immutable ordered collections. Sequence operations let programs work with groups of values instead of individual variables.
codeExample:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
numbers.append(40)
first, second, *rest = numbers
print(first, rest)
howItWorks: Use lists when the collection should change.
Use tuples for fixed records or values that should not be mutated.
Indexing starts at zero.
Unpacking can make data flow clearer when the number of values is known.
fullExample:
items = ["pen", "book", "mouse"]
items.append("keyboard")
items.remove("pen")
print(items)
print(items[:2])
practiceTask: Build a shopping-list program that adds items, removes one item, prints the number of items, and displays the first two items.

title: Dictionaries and Sets
summary: Model structured records with dictionaries and remove duplicates efficiently with sets.
definition: Dictionaries map keys to values and are ideal for named fields and lookup tables. Sets contain unique elements and support fast membership-style operations.
howItWorks: Dictionary keys must be hashable and are used for lookup.
Use get() when a missing key should have a default.
Sets automatically remove duplicates.
Choose a data structure based on the operations your program needs.
practiceTask: Create a product catalog dictionary and a set of unique categories. Look up a missing product safely and print the unique categories.
starterCode:

title: Comprehensions and Data Transformation
summary: Transform and filter collections with list, set, and dictionary comprehensions.
definition: Comprehensions provide a compact way to build collections from iterables. They are powerful when the transformation remains readable; complex logic should usually use normal loops or helper functions.
howItWorks: A comprehension contains an output expression, an iteration, and optional filtering.
Dictionary comprehensions build key-value mappings.
Keep comprehensions readable; nested or complicated comprehensions can hurt maintainability.
Comprehensions create new collections rather than modifying the source.
fullExample:
words = ["python", "code", "developer", "api"]
lengths = {word: len(word) for word in words}
long_words = [word for word in words if len(word) >= 4]
print(lengths)
print(long_words)

title: Arguments, *args, **kwargs and Closures
summary: Write flexible functions and understand positional, keyword, variadic arguments, and closures.
definition: Python functions can accept positional arguments, keyword arguments, arbitrary *args, and arbitrary **kwargs. Closures retain access to variables from an enclosing scope.
howItWorks: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
Keyword-only parameters can make APIs clearer.
A closure is an inner function that remembers values from its enclosing scope.
practiceTask: Create a function that accepts any number of scores and keyword metadata, then return a structured report. Add a closure that creates a reusable percentage calculator.

title: Modules, Imports, Virtual Environments and Dependencies
summary: Organize code into modules and understand venv, pip, requirements, and import boundaries.
definition: A professional Python project separates responsibilities across modules and uses an isolated virtual environment for dependencies. pip installs packages into that environment; a requirements file records dependencies.
codeExample:
import math
from pathlib import Path

print(math.sqrt(81))
print(Path(".").resolve())
howItWorks: A module is a Python file that can be imported.
Prefer explicit imports and avoid circular dependencies.
Use python -m venv .venv to create an isolated environment.
Use pip install to add dependencies and pip freeze or a curated requirements file to reproduce environments.
fullExample:

title: Files, pathlib, JSON and CSV
summary: Read and write files safely and exchange structured data using JSON and CSV.
definition: File I/O persists data beyond a program run. pathlib provides readable cross-platform paths; JSON represents nested structured data; CSV represents rows and columns.
codeExample:
from pathlib import Path
import json

path = Path("profile.json")
data = {"name": "Sam", "level": 2}
path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
print(json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
howItWorks: Use pathlib instead of manually joining path strings.
Specify text encoding explicitly for predictable files.
JSON is useful for structured application data.
CSV is useful for tabular data and should be parsed with Python's csv module when possible.
fullExample:
from pathlib import Path
import json

path = Path("data.json")
data = {"tasks": ["learn", "build"], "done": 1}
path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
loaded = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(loaded)

title: Exceptions, Validation and Debugging
summary: Handle expected failures cleanly and debug programs systematically.
definition: Exceptions represent abnormal conditions such as invalid input or missing files. Professional code catches specific exceptions at the boundary where it can recover and lets unexpected errors remain visible.
howItWorks: Catch specific exceptions instead of using a broad except by default.
Use else for code that should run only when no exception occurred and finally for cleanup.
Validate inputs before dangerous operations when practical.
Debug by reproducing the problem, reducing it, inspecting state, and testing the smallest fix.
practiceTask: Write a safe integer parser that rejects invalid text and negative values. Deliberately introduce one bug, reproduce it, and document the debugging steps you used to fix it.

title: Testing with unittest/pytest Concepts
summary: Turn requirements into repeatable tests and learn assertions, fixtures, edge cases, and testable design.
definition: Tests are executable checks of behavior. Unit tests should be small, deterministic, and focused. pytest is a common professional framework; unittest is included in Python's standard library.
codeExample:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

assert add(2, 3) == 5
assert add(-1, 1) == 0
howItWorks: Test normal cases, boundaries, invalid input, and important regressions.
Assertions state what must be true.
pytest discovers test_*.py files and provides concise test syntax and fixtures.
Small pure functions are easier to test than functions that mix input, business logic, and output.
fullExample:
def is_even(number):
    return number % 2 == 0

assert is_even(4)
assert not is_even(5)
assert is_even(0)
print("Basic checks passed")

title: Classes, Dataclasses and Encapsulation
summary: Model domain objects with classes, dataclasses, methods, properties, and clear state.
definition: Classes define behavior and state for objects. dataclasses reduce boilerplate for data-focused objects. Encapsulation means controlling how state is changed rather than exposing arbitrary mutation.
codeExample:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float

item = Product("Book", 12.5)
print(item)
howItWorks: __init__ and other dunder methods define object behavior.
Methods operate on instance state through self.
Dataclasses generate common methods such as __init__ and __repr__.
Properties can enforce rules around access without exposing implementation details.
practiceTask: Design a small domain class such as Task, Product, or BankAccount. Give it validated state and at least three methods, then add assertions for its important behavior.

title: Composition, Inheritance and Polymorphism
summary: Choose composition or inheritance deliberately and use polymorphism through shared interfaces.
definition: Inheritance models an is-a relationship, but composition often produces more flexible systems. Polymorphism lets code call the same method on different objects without checking every concrete type.
howItWorks: Use inheritance when subclasses genuinely satisfy the parent contract.
Use composition when one object owns or delegates to another object.
Polymorphism reduces type-specific branching.
super() calls inherited behavior and should be used with a clear design.
practiceTask: Create two interchangeable storage or notification implementations and one function that uses either without checking its concrete type.

title: Iterators, Generators and Lazy Work
summary: Understand the iterator protocol and use generators to process data without storing everything at once.
definition: An iterable can produce items; an iterator keeps iteration state and provides __next__. Generators use yield to create iterators lazily, which can reduce memory use for large streams.
howItWorks: iter() obtains an iterator and next() requests its next value.
Generators pause at yield and resume later.
Lazy pipelines are useful for large files, streams, and transformations.
Do not convert a huge lazy sequence to a list unless you actually need all values at once.
practiceTask: Write a generator that yields only valid positive numbers from a sequence of text lines. Explain why it uses less memory than building a complete result list.

title: Decorators and Context Managers
summary: Use decorators for reusable cross-cutting behavior and context managers for reliable resource cleanup.
definition: A decorator wraps a callable to add behavior without changing its core implementation. A context manager guarantees setup/cleanup around a block, commonly through with.
howItWorks: functools.wraps preserves useful metadata from the wrapped function.
Decorators are useful for logging, timing, authorization, caching, and validation.
with blocks make resource lifecycle explicit.
Files and locks should be cleaned up even when an exception occurs.
practiceTask: Write a timing or logging decorator that returns the original function result. Then use a context manager to guarantee cleanup of a simple resource-like object.

title: Type Hints, Protocols and Documentation
summary: Make code easier to understand and maintain with annotations, modern typing, docstrings, and contracts.
definition: Type hints document intended data shapes and help editors and static type checkers catch mistakes. They do not normally enforce types at runtime. Good docstrings explain purpose, parameters, return values, and important behavior.
howItWorks: Annotate parameters and return values for public functions.
Use built-in generics such as list[str] on modern Python.
Protocols can describe behavior rather than requiring inheritance.
Type hints are most valuable when paired with clear names, tests, and tooling such as mypy or pyright.
practiceTask: Add type hints and useful docstrings to three functions from earlier lessons. Identify one incorrect call that a static checker should flag.

title: HTTP APIs, JSON and Integration
summary: Consume web APIs safely, parse JSON, handle status codes, and separate network code from business logic.
definition: An HTTP API exposes resources through requests and responses. Professional clients check status codes, set timeouts, parse JSON deliberately, and isolate external I/O so the rest of the application remains testable.
codeExample:
import json

payload = '{"name": "Python", "level": "advanced"}'
data = json.loads(payload)
print(data["name"])
howItWorks: HTTP methods communicate intent: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
Always use a timeout for network calls in real clients.
Check response status before trusting response data.
Keep API transport code separate from parsing and business rules so it can be tested with fake responses.
practiceTask: Design an API client function with a timeout, status handling, JSON parsing, and a separate function that turns the response into application data. The browser runner may not allow live network access, so use a mocked response for the exercise.

title: SQLite and SQL CRUD
summary: Persist application data with SQLite and understand tables, queries, parameters, transactions, and CRUD.
definition: SQLite is a small relational database included with Python. SQL describes data operations; parameterized queries keep values separate from SQL text and reduce injection risk.
codeExample:
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE tasks (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)")
connection.execute("INSERT INTO tasks (title) VALUES (?)", ("Learn SQL",))
for row in connection.execute("SELECT id, title FROM tasks"):
    print(row)
connection.close()
howItWorks: Tables store rows with a defined schema.
SELECT reads data; INSERT creates; UPDATE changes; DELETE removes.
Use placeholders such as ? and pass parameters separately.
Commit intentional writes and close connections; context managers can simplify transaction handling.
fullExample:
import sqlite3

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as db:
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)")
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", ("Sam",))
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM users").fetchall()
    print(rows)
practiceTask: Design a CRUD layer for tasks with create, list, update, and delete functions. Use parameterized SQL and return Python data structures instead of printing from the database layer.

title: Asyncio, Concurrency and I/O
summary: Understand async/await, tasks, concurrency choices, and when parallel work is appropriate.
definition: Concurrency is about making progress on multiple tasks. asyncio is designed for cooperative I/O concurrency; threads can help with blocking I/O; processes can use multiple CPU cores for CPU-bound work.
codeExample:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return f"done: {name}"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("A"), fetch("B"))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
howItWorks: async def defines a coroutine function; calling it creates a coroutine.
await yields control while waiting for asynchronous work.
asyncio.gather can run independent coroutines concurrently.
Choose asyncio for async-friendly I/O, threads for compatible blocking I/O, and processes for CPU-heavy work.
fullExample:
import asyncio

async def job(number):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    return number * 2

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(job(n) for n in range(5)))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
practiceTask: Create three async jobs and run them concurrently with asyncio.gather. Explain why concurrency can reduce waiting time for I/O but does not magically speed up CPU-heavy Python code.

title: Logging, Configuration and Security Basics
summary: Build software that can be diagnosed safely with logging, configuration, environment variables, and basic security habits.
definition: Production programs need observable behavior without leaking secrets. Logging records useful events; configuration separates environment-specific settings; secrets should not be hard-coded; validation and least privilege reduce risk.
codeExample:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info("Application started")
howItWorks: Use logging instead of print for operational diagnostics.
Keep secrets such as API keys out of source code and repositories.
Validate external input and use parameterized database queries.
Fail safely: do not expose stack traces, credentials, or sensitive data to end users.
fullExample:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s:%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

user = "Sam"
logger.info("Processing user %s", user)
print("Done")

title: CLI Applications, Packaging and Dependency Management
summary: Build a clean command-line interface and understand how professional Python packages are structured and distributed.
definition: A CLI turns a program into a reusable tool. argparse provides standard command-line parsing. Packaging metadata tells Python tooling how to install and build a project. A clean src/ layout separates package code from tests and tooling.
codeExample:
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Task tool")
parser.add_argument("--name", default="world")
args = parser.parse_args()
print(f"Hello {args.name}")
howItWorks: argparse validates and documents command-line arguments.
Keep CLI parsing at the boundary and call reusable application functions underneath.
Use pyproject.toml for modern package metadata and tooling configuration.
Pin or constrain dependencies appropriately and keep development dependencies separate from runtime dependencies.
fullExample:
import argparse

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--name", default="world")
args = parser.parse_args()
print(greet(args.name))
practiceTask: Design a CLI with subcommands such as add, list, and remove. Keep the CLI thin and put business logic in importable functions that can be tested without command-line parsing.

title: Architecture, Refactoring and Maintainability
summary: Turn working code into maintainable code using separation of concerns, dependency injection, and refactoring.
definition: Architecture is how responsibilities and dependencies are organized. Separate domain logic from I/O, inject dependencies when useful, and refactor in small tested steps rather than rewriting blindly.
howItWorks: Keep business rules independent from databases, HTTP clients, and user interfaces when practical.
Dependency injection makes components replaceable and easier to test.
Refactor behavior-preserving changes in small steps.
Prefer simple architecture that matches the project's size; abstraction is not a goal by itself.
practiceTask: Take one earlier project design and split it into at least three responsibilities: input/CLI, domain/business logic, and persistence/output. Write down what dependency can be replaced in tests.

title: Performance, Complexity and Profiling
summary: Reason about time and memory costs and measure performance before optimizing.
definition: Performance work starts with measurement. Big-O notation describes how work grows with input size; profiling identifies real bottlenecks. Optimize the bottleneck that matters, not code based on guesses.
codeExample:
import time

start = time.perf_counter()
total = sum(range(1_000_000))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(total, f"{elapsed:.4f}s")
howItWorks: A list membership check is generally linear; a set lookup is designed for fast average membership.
Nested loops often increase growth dramatically.
Use time.perf_counter for elapsed timing and cProfile for broader profiling.
Memory usage matters too; generators can avoid building large intermediate collections.
fullExample:
import time

values = list(range(100_000))
start = time.perf_counter()
result = sum(values)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print("sum:", result)
print("seconds:", round(elapsed, 6))
practiceTask: Compare two implementations of a data-processing task, measure them, and explain the trade-off. Do not claim an optimization until your measurement supports it.

title: Professional Review: Build, Test and Ship
summary: Integrate Python language skills, engineering practices, testing, persistence, APIs, and clean architecture into one production-style workflow.
definition: A professional Python developer does more than write syntax: they clarify requirements, design data and boundaries, handle failures, test behavior, manage dependencies, protect secrets, log useful events, and refactor code for maintainability.
howItWorks: Start from requirements and acceptance criteria.
Design small testable functions and explicit data models.
Choose persistence, APIs, concurrency, and abstractions only where the problem needs them.
Before calling a project finished, test normal and failure paths, review security, check logs, measure important performance, and document how to run it.

title: Project 3: JSON Expense Tracker
summary: Apply data structures, comprehensions, files, JSON, exceptions, and testing to a useful local application.
definition: Build a local expense tracker that stores expenses in JSON. Users can add, list, summarize, filter, and remove expenses. The program should survive a restart because data is persisted to a file.
codeExample:
expense = {"category": "food", "amount": 12.5}
print(expense)
howItWorks: Represent each expense as structured data.
Load and save JSON through a small persistence layer.
Validate amounts and categories at the input boundary.
Use functions for add/list/summary operations and test them with in-memory data where possible.
fullExample:
expenses = [
    {"category": "food", "amount": 12.5},
    {"category": "travel", "amount": 8.0},
]
food = [e for e in expenses if e["category"] == "food"]
print(sum(e["amount"] for e in food))
practiceTask: Implement add, list, total, category summary, and delete. Persist to JSON, handle a missing/corrupt file, and write tests for the core calculations.

title: Project 4: SQLite Task Manager CLI
summary: Combine OOP, SQLite, type hints, testing, CLI design, and clean architecture.
definition: Build a command-line task manager backed by SQLite. The program should support add, list, complete, and delete operations. Keep database access separate from business logic and command-line parsing.
codeExample:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE tasks (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL)")
print("Database ready")
howItWorks: Create a repository/data-access layer for SQL operations.
Create a service layer for task rules.
Use typed domain objects where useful.
Expose the service through argparse commands and test it with an isolated database.
fullExample:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Task:
    id: int
    title: str
    done: bool = False

print(Task(1, "Learn SQLite"))
practiceTask: Implement the full CLI with parameterized SQL, clear errors, tests, type hints, and a README explaining installation and usage.
starterCode:

title: Project 5: Production-Style Python Application
summary: Integrate the professional engineering skills from the complete 30-day path into one substantial application.
definition: Build one application that solves a real problem you care about. It must have clear requirements, modular architecture, persistent data where appropriate, tests, logging, configuration, validation, documentation, and a measurable quality/performance check.
howItWorks: Write requirements and acceptance criteria first.
Design modules around responsibilities and dependencies.
Use type hints, tests, error handling, logging, and secure configuration.
Choose SQLite, an API, or async I/O only if the application needs it.
Finish with a code review checklist and documented run/test commands.
practiceTask: Ship a complete application with a README, tests, typed core logic, persistence or an external API when relevant, structured logging, configuration, security review, performance measurement, and a clean CLI or user-facing entry point. Do not mark it complete until every requirement is demonstrated.
